sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dzongs: the centre of temporal and religious authorities
sources.note: Original UNESCO-hosted tentative-list submission by the Bhutan National Commission for UNESCO checked, especially lines 80-101. It dates Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal's arrival to 1616, describes fortress building and unification, and explains the later religious and administrative uses of dzongs. UNESCO warns that the State Party is responsible for the account and that publication does not validate boundaries.

sources.title: Royal Education Council of Bhutan, Class V Social Studies textbook, 2024
sources.note: Original government curriculum PDF checked, p. 28: arrival through Gasa in 1616, political unification, dzong construction, taxation and compulsory labour, the Chhoe-sid dual system in 1651, Je Khenpo and Desi offices, and Zhabdrung's death in 1651. The textbook's celebratory judgments are not adopted.

sources.title: Royal Government of Bhutan, Bhutan Architectural Guidelines, section on dzongs
sources.note: Original Ministry architectural-guidelines PDF checked: dzongs as strategically placed fortresses, continuing administrative and monastic centres, and repositories of paintings, carvings, manuscripts and textiles. The card treats these as living institutions with changing uses, not frozen medieval scenery.

sources.title: National Museum of Bhutan, National Museum at a Glance
sources.note: Original National Museum history checked, paragraphs on repeated Tibetan invasions and internal opposition, Paro Ta Dzong built in 1649, 2.5-metre walls, and tunnels that supplied water and provisions in wartime. Its incorrect statement that the first king was enthroned in 1919 is not used.

sources.title: Royal Bhutanese Embassy, New Delhi, History of Bhutan
sources.note: Original Bhutan foreign-ministry page checked: dual government, its weakening in the later eighteenth century, regional discord, Ugyen Wangchuck's election as first hereditary monarch in 1907, and the first parliamentary election in 2008. Royal praise is treated as the government's perspective rather than independent evaluation.

sources.title: Bumthang Dzongkhag Administration, brief history of Bumthang
sources.note: Original local-government chronology checked: the 1864-1865 Duar War, Jigme Namgyal's rise, Ugyen Wangchuck's gains after civil wars and political conflicts in 1882-1885, and the 1907 monarchy. Used for dated regional events, not its broad heritage praise.

sources.title: Library of Congress Federal Research Division, Nepal and Bhutan: Country Studies
sources.note: Institutional historical study checked, Bhutan chapter pp. 260-261: five-month Duar War of 1864-1865, Bhutanese battlefield successes and final defeat, and the 11 November 1865 Treaty of Sinchula ceding the Assam and Bengal Duars and Dewangiri for an annual subsidy. The study represents its scholarly authors, not an official United States policy.

sources.title: Ministry of External Affairs, Government of India, Treaty between India and Bhutan, 1949
sources.note: Original treaty text checked, preamble and Articles 1-2: perpetual peace, Indian non-interference in internal administration, and Bhutan's agreement to be guided by Indian advice in external relations. The card does not soften that unequal foreign-relations clause.

sources.title: Ministry of External Affairs, Government of India, India-Bhutan Friendship Treaty, 2007
sources.note: Original treaty text checked: signed 8 February 2007, in force 2 March 2007, updating the 1949 treaty; preamble reaffirms independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, and Article 2 calls for close cooperation without the 1949 advice clause.

sources.title: Parliament of Bhutan, History of Parliament
sources.note: Original current Parliament history checked: National Assembly established in 1953, Royal Advisory Council in 1965, legislative supremacy in 1968, elected local institutions in 1981 and 1991, transfer of executive power to elected ministers in 1998, constitutional drafting from 2001, and bicameral parliamentary democracy in 2008.

sources.title: Parliament of Bhutan and UNDP, Ten Years of Democracy in Bhutan, 2019
sources.note: Original joint Parliament-UNDP report checked, PDF pp. 19-29 and 50-57: 1907 monarchy, emancipation of enslaved people in 1956, institutional reforms, 2001-2008 constitutional process, 24 March 2008 election and 18 July adoption. Praise and retrospective democratic narratives are identified as such rather than accepted uncritically.

sources.title: Permanent Mission of Bhutan to the United Nations, Bhutan and the UN
sources.note: Original foreign-ministry mission page checked: gradual outside engagement from the early 1960s, admission to the United Nations on 21 September 1971, and later multilateral participation. Used for dates and Bhutan's stated rationale, not for self-evaluation.

sources.title: Parliament of Bhutan, Constitution of the Kingdom of Bhutan
sources.note: Original official bilingual Constitution checked: adopted 18 July 2008; Article 1 on sovereignty, democratic constitutional monarchy, twenty dzongkhags, Dzongkha and separated branches; Article 2 on the King; Article 5(3) on sixty percent forest cover; and Article 9 on education and health.

sources.title: Parliament of Bhutan, System of Government
sources.note: Original current Parliament page checked: democratic constitutional monarchy since 2008, King as head of state, prime minister and cabinet exercising executive authority, bicameral Parliament, and separate judiciary. Used as an institutional description, not a rating of democratic quality.

sources.title: Election Commission of Bhutan, fourth National Assembly general-election results
sources.note: Original Election Commission declaration checked: 9 January 2024 election, People's Democratic Party 30 seats, Bhutan Tendrel Party 17, 65.6 percent turnout, 326,775 votes and 809 polling stations. Seat totals are reported as the declaration's dated result, not guaranteed current composition.

sources.title: Prime Minister's Office of Bhutan, current government
sources.note: Original PMO page checked on 27 September 2026. It identifies Tshering Tobgay as head of the current government for 2024-2028 and records his January 2024 return to office. Biographical praise and award claims are not used.

sources.title: National Assembly of Bhutan, joint parliamentary-visit release, 17 May 2026
sources.note: Original National Assembly release checked on 27 September 2026. Its account of the 13-15 May 2026 visit identifies Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck as King of Bhutan and records the delegation's royal audience. Used only for the time-bounded officeholder identification.

sources.title: UNHCR, Turning waste into wealth: a refugee's story of resilience and climate action, 20 January 2025
sources.note: Original current UNHCR field story checked: Amber Bahadur Jogi is identified as Lhotshampa, a Nepali-speaking minority member born in Gelephu who fled with tens of thousands in the early 1990s; 113,500 Bhutanese refugees were resettled to third countries in 2007-2016. One family story is not generalized beyond the dated programme totals.

sources.title: Centre for Bhutan and GNH Studies, GNH 2022 survey report
sources.note: Original national survey report checked, especially methodology pp. 23-27, Table 3 p. 27, trends pp. 63-64 and policy chapters. The index uses nine equal domains and 33 weighted indicators with a 66 percent sufficiency cutoff; 2022 index 0.781, 48.1 percent deeply or extensively happy, and 51.9 percent not-yet-happy. It also counts unpaid cooking, cleaning and childcare within work time.

sources.title: United Nations Committee for Development Policy, Bhutan LDC profile
sources.note: Original UN country profile checked: Bhutan entered the least developed country category in 1971 and graduated on 13 December 2023; the page links the 2024 and 2025 monitoring reports and transition documents. Graduation is treated as a threshold-based classification change, not proof that poverty or economic vulnerability vanished.

sources.title: National Statistics Bureau of Bhutan, third-quarter Socio-Economic Indicators 2025
sources.note: Original official statistical bulletin checked, forestry table p. 17: 69.7 percent forest cover, excluding alpine shrubs and shrubs, and 43.48 percent protected area. The card preserves the definition note and pairs the statistic with the constitutional floor rather than a carbon-negative slogan.

sources.title: Bhutan Department of Tourism, About Bhutan
sources.note: Original official tourism page checked: city work and markets, rural butter churning, gathering wild greens, and conversation over suja or butter tea. These are illustrative scenes selected for visitors, not a census of every household or region.

sources.title: Bhutan Department of Tourism, Adventure experiences and traditional sports
sources.note: Original official tourism page checked: archery as national sport and social festival game, traditional hard-bamboo bows, teams shooting at targets about 145 metres away, and songs and dances around play. Gender and alcohol descriptions on the page are historical-tourism generalizations and are not turned into rules for all families.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Mask dance of the drums from Drametse
sources.note: Original UNESCO element page checked: twice-yearly Drametse community festival, sixteen masked dancers, ten musicians, peaceful and wrathful sequences, nineteenth-century spread to other places, and declining practitioner numbers. The page title is correct despite the legacy URL slug saying vimbuza.

sources.title: National Museum of Bhutan, Third Floor collection
sources.note: Original National Museum collection page checked: distinct Brokpa, Layap, western and central dance costumes; kira described as a wrapped women's dress fastened at shoulders and waist, and gho as a men's robe raised and belted at the waist. The card emphasizes regional and personal variation.

sources.title: Dzongkha Development Commission, Acts, rules and regulations
sources.note: Original official Dzongkha publication page checked. It prints the Constitution title as འབྲུག་གི་རྩ་ཁྲིམས་ཆེན་མོ། and links the official text. The card gives a conservative Wylie-style romanization and an English title translation, not a claim about a single pronunciation.

sources.title: Dzongkha Development Commission, history of the Commission
sources.note: Original official page checked in Dzongkha: it states that Bhutan has more than nineteen languages, that Dzongkha long served administration, that it was declared the national language in 1971, and that materials and technical standards were developed for schools and computing. The English précis in the card is editorial.

sources.title: Royal Government of Bhutan, Tertiary Education Policy of the Kingdom of Bhutan, 2010
sources.note: Original Ministry of Education policy checked, p. 1: centuries of monastic education, schools at Bumthang and Haa in 1915, organized modern education from the late 1950s, and Royal University of Bhutan established in 2003. Article 9 education language is quoted there, but the card avoids treating policy aspiration as complete access.

sources.title: Bhutan Council for School Examinations and Assessment and UNICEF, National Education Assessment 2024
sources.note: Original official assessment factsheet checked: representative samples of 4,633 Grade III and 4,810 Grade VI pupils; more than 90 percent minimum proficiency in Grade VI English literacy but only 36 percent in mathematics; disability, income and early-childhood attendance gaps; and student screen-use and wellbeing results. Sample scope is retained.

sources.title: Royal Government of Bhutan Ministry of Health, history of health services
sources.note: Original Ministry page checked: older Sowa Rigpa practice, first Bhutanese MBBS doctor in the 1950s, planned services beginning with a one-room dispensary, two hospitals and eleven dispensaries by 1961, and formal integration of traditional medicine in 1967. Current facility totals on this undated history page are not used.

sources.title: UNICEF Bhutan, When every dose is made to count, 27 April 2026
sources.note: Original dated field story checked: Punakha family and health workers, national immunization beginning in 1979, over 42,000 children and adolescents vaccinated in 2025, 99.5 percent pregnancy protection against tetanus and diphtheria, and vaccine storage at 2-8 degrees Celsius with twice-daily checks. Individual quotations are not generalized.

sources.title: Royal Government of Bhutan and UNICEF, World Water Day report release, 22 March 2026
sources.note: Original joint release checked: National Water and Sanitation Report 2025 finds nearly universal basic sanitation and 90 percent safely managed sanitation, while 51.2 percent had safely managed drinking water; dried and drying sources in Paro and Thimphu and unequal water-collection burdens are also recorded. A future universal-access target is not presented as achieved.

sources.title: Royal Government of Bhutan and UNICEF, inclusive school toilet release, 22 March 2024
sources.note: Original joint release checked: open-defecation-free status, eighth UNICEF-supported special-education school toilet, 287 pupils benefiting across supported school facilities, five monastic-school toilets benefiting 335 children, and official acknowledgment that toilet quality, quantity and safety gaps remain.

proposedOverrides.summary: Bhutan from seventeenth-century unification and living dzongs to a modern constitutional monarchy.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Exact open Kingdom of Bhutan record only. The imported civilization begins at 1650 and stays open, while the unification process began after Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal arrived in 1616 and the dual government took definite form in 1651. Do not merge the separate coarse `bhutan` record dated 1200-1279: it has a different seven-vertex polygon with bounds [89.57429574295742,24.767871062662792,94.49194491944922,27.668302953792008] and no demonstrated continuous identity link in the atlas metadata. The `bhutan-1650` record has eighteen imported historical intervals. The same 18-vertex shape repeats from 1650 through 1783; the 1783-1800 feature abruptly becomes an eight-vertex coarse polygon; later intervals use 18 or 27 vertices with minor quantization changes. The open modern feature covers 2020-2100, has 13 vertices and bounds [88.814,26.719,92.104,28.296]. Tested inside it: Thimphu, Punakha, Paro, Trongsa, Trashigang and Gelephu. Tested outside: Gangtok, Guwahati and Lhasa. The same sketch incorrectly excludes tested Samtse and includes tested Tawang, so it cannot be treated as a legal or dispute-sensitive boundary. Polygon changes do not establish conquest, cession or collapse without external evidence.
